newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends firmer on supply concerns.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends firmer on supply concerns.

text.p: COMEX copper surged higher again on Wednesday, hitting a six-week high before easing slightly as shortcovering, concerns over physical tightness and a clutch of potential supply problems underpinned prices, traders said.
The cash premium over three months contract on LME widened further to $160/$170.
May COMEX settled 2.90 cents firmer at 112.80 cents per pound, traded 113.70 to 110.00 cents. Spot April went out 3.15 cents higher at 113.65 cents.
Volume was heavy at an estimated 18,000 lots.

Many brokers believed the surge was linked to the physical market rather than purely shortcovering. Much of the backwardation was located nearby, in the cash to May period, which usually indicated physical tightness rather than fund shortcovering.
"There is some physical tightness in the U.S., Europe and the Far East. The statistics are looking phenomenol as far as consumption is concerned," Fred Demler of E D and F Man said.
LME stocks continue to fall, down 1,025 tonnes on Wednesday to 149,100 tonnes.
COMEX stocks rose 1,448 short tons Wednesday to 50,181 tons. More metal is expected to flow in from LME depots following arbitrage deals.
Earlier brokers said there had been some good arbitrage with buying of LME July and selling its COMEX counterpart. LME cash moved into a 1.2 cent premium over spot COMEX.
Several issues are dogging copper supply.
Striking workers at Escondida mine in Chile vote again Wednesday on whether to accept the company's labor deal.

The Kennecott smelter in Utah will stop producing blister for another five weeks, and the United Steelworkers and Phelps Dodge appear no nearer to agreement on a new Chino mine labor deal ahead of meetings Thursday and Friday.
"The market is due for some consolidation, but chart-wise it looks quite strong, and I think it's going to make another test of contract highs," Demler said.
Surging copper prices this week has rekindled the U.S. scrap market as dealers who held on to material in anticipation of higher tags, began selling, scrap merchants said.
